finding.title: Tool-free direct Ollama sessions are counted as live workstation code, holding paired-device changes
finding.scenario: A workstation starts a direct (non-Mission) Ollama task. Direct tasks carry no executionScope (bunny-host/manager.server.ts:668 sets executionScope only when a scope is supplied), so providerSessionAuthority('ollama', undefined) returns null (authorization.server.ts:196 rejects any access other than read/write). liveCodeExecutions() therefore treats the tool-free session as shell code and returns it. While it runs, remoteMutationHeld() (manager.server.ts:2322) returns a desktopRequired hold for every paired-device mutation (inert filesystem.write, delete, git changes), so the device cannot complete its approved step until the Ollama task ends or the workstation answers. Fail-closed and availability-only; no code execution is granted.
finding.evidence: Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, own temp folder): providerSessionAuthority('ollama', undefined) -> null; providerSessionAuthority('ollama','write') -> 'tool_free'; providerSessionAuthority('claude','read') -> 'read_tools'. Session registration at bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1383 (this.sessions.set for every started session). Not run end-to-end.
finding.recommendation: In liveCodeExecutions, treat a session as tool-free when task.provider === 'ollama' and task.mission is absent (direct local inference has no tools), or pass 'tool_free' explicitly for direct Ollama tasks. Keep the fail-closed default for unknown providers and for db.get failures.

votes.reasoning: Claim verified, not refuted. Mechanism: direct (non-Mission) tasks get no executionScope (bunny-host/manager.server.ts:668, `scope ? {access} : undefined`), so providerSessionAuthority(task.provider, undefined) returns null (authorization.server.ts, access check precedes the provider check). liveCodeExecutions (manager.server.ts:2311-2319) maps null to a live "session" entry, and remoteMutationHeld (manager.server.ts:2322-2333) turns that into a desktopRequired ask for every paired-device Mission mutation (bus.server.ts:165-166). Probe in a mkdtemp folder (deleted afterward): ollama/undefined -> null, ollama/write -> tool_free, ollama/read -> tool_free, claude/read -> read_tools, codex/undefined -> null. The Ollama adapter is a tool-free POST /api/generate (adapters.server.ts:52, 133-168), so the classification is over-conservative, not a real shell path. Sessions register at bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1383 and are removed at :1645. No allow path is opened: the hold only adds an ask, and no device-side action gains authority. Only workstation-started direct Ollama tasks trigger it, since devices cannot create direct tasks (http.server.ts submit path is the workstation route). It is therefore an availability and misleading-message defect, fail-closed, not a security problem. Not one of the listed dispositions, so it is not refuted. Severity LOW matches. The recommended fix (treat provider==='ollama' with no mission as tool_free, keep the default fail-closed for other providers and db.get failures) is sound. Test-results files were not touched; no repo tests were run.

Not refuted. The mechanism is real and I confirmed it by reading and probing; the finding is availability/correctness only, so LOW is the right severity.

Code path checked:
- manager.server.ts:2311-2320 liveCodeExecutions() takes every id in this.tasks.sessions (and lingering keys). For each it calls providerSessionAuthority(task.provider, task.executionScope?.access) and only returns [] for "tool_free" or "read_tools". Any null result becomes a live-code entry.
- bunny-host/manager.server.ts:665-668: a direct task gets executionScope only when a scope is supplied. Direct Ollama tasks therefore have no scope. Line 1383 registers every started session in this.sessions, so a direct Ollama task counts as live code.
- authorization.server.ts (providerSessionAuthority): the access check runs first, so access undefined returns null before the ollama branch is reached.
- Probe in a mkdtemp folder (deleted afterwards): providerSessionAuthority('ollama', undefined) -> null; ('ollama','write') -> tool_free; ('claude','read') -> read_tools. This matches the finding.
- The Ollama adapter (adapters.server.ts:133-176) only issues an HTTP generation via execute() and has pid() => null. It never uses executionScope and has no tools, so the null classification is wrong for Ollama.
- bus.server.ts:165 and manager.server.ts:2322-2332: remoteMutationHeld applies to Mission-attributed, non-direct MUTATIONS from remote actors. While the Ollama task runs, those device mutations return desktopRequired holds. The hold ends when the Ollama task ends, and generation has a timeout, so it is not indefinite.

Why it is not a security issue: no code execution is granted, and the device still cannot act outside its envelope. The hold only delays. The finding's own wording, "fail-closed and availability-only", is accurate. It is not one of the listed owner-policy dispositions or accepted limitations, though, and it is not exactly a fail-closed-by-design case. Policy says tool-free Ollama is a permitted device-adjacent operation, and this code blocks unrelated device mutations because of a missing scope on a session that cannot run tools. The "code approved on the Windows Host is running (ollama session ...)" message is also inaccurate for a tool-free session.

The recommended fix is correct but should be scoped to Ollama only. For direct Claude or Codex tasks with no scope, the null is correct: those launch with full tools, so they must stay fail-closed. Test run: none; no repo files were modified and test-results/ is untouched.

finding.title: computer.open_app Calculator launch is remotely approvable without naming the Calculator window
finding.scenario: remoteCalculatorOperation() accepts action === 'computer.open_app' without requiring params.title === 'Calculator', so a device can approve {app:'calculator'}. The round-7 policy text says exact reviewed Calculator operations must name the Calculator window. The launch target is fixed (computer.server.ts:13 maps calculator to calc.exe) and target params are rejected by calculatorOperation, so the practical risk is low; this is a literal deviation from the stated contract, not an escape.
finding.recommendation: Either document open_app as a deliberate exception in the owner contract or drop the open_app exemption so the policy wording holds exactly.

finding.title: Inert-extension files written by a paired device execute as code when a workstation-approved command runs them
finding.scenario: A paired device, under a remote envelope, writes notes.txt containing JavaScript. filesystem.write to a .txt path passes remoteExecutionRefusal (INERT_DATA_FILE at line 126 accepts .txt/.md/.log/.csv/.yaml, and inertDataPath at line 156 returns true). Later the workstation approves an ordinary terminal.exec of `node notes.txt`. The review gate (bus.server.ts:169-172) asks, but the prompt only names the path ("this runs code over files changed under paired-device authority (...\notes.txt)"), not the content. After allow_once the device-authored code runs. Node runs a .txt or .log file as JavaScript via `node file` and via require(); Python 3.12 runs a .md file as Python. The contract that device-placed code cannot be loaded by any later or already-running process is therefore false for interpreters.
finding.evidence: Probe (throwaway, repo not modified): device mission approved with remote authority wrote notes.txt = `require("node:fs").writeFileSync("PWNED.txt", ...)`; workstation mission terminal.exec {command:"node",args:["notes.txt"]} asked with desktopRequired:true and reason naming notes.txt; after respond(allow_once,'workstation') the mission completed and PWNED.txt existed. remoteExecutionRefusal("filesystem.write",{path:"notes.txt"},"WRITE",root) returned null; data.log and p.md also null; loader.cjs refused. Direct check: `node notes.txt` and `require('./data.log')` each executed the JS; `python p.md` executed Python. Session-level paths are not required for the trigger.
finding.recommendation: Do not treat extension as proof of inertness. Either (a) bind any code-running request whose argv, cwd or require graph names a pending device-changed file to a desktop-only ask that shows the file's digest and contents, or (b) refuse terminal/session runs whose arguments name files changed under remote authority unless the workstation answer names that exact content digest. Update the (A) contract and the accepted-limitation text, which currently assume device-written inert files cannot be loaded as code.

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted; the claim holds, but I would downgrade it from BLOCKER to HIGH.

Verified in code (no repo files edited, no probes run):
- src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts:126 INERT_DATA_FILE matches notes.txt, data.log, p.md. inertDataPath (~line 156) returns true for them. remoteExecutionRefusal (lines 226-233) therefore returns null for a device filesystem.write to these names, so the write is allowed under remote authority.
- Node runs a .txt file as CommonJS JavaScript when given as an argument or loaded via require(). Python runs a .md file as source when given as the script argument. So the (A) contract ("nothing it writes can be loaded and run as code later") is false for these interpreters.
- The only barrier after the write is the review gate. bus.server.ts:169-172 asks for any runsCode request (terminal.exec always qualifies) when pendingRemoteChanges is non-empty. manager.server.ts:2303-2312 (pendingRemoteReview) builds the prompt from paths only; store.server.ts:158 returns only path/root/actor/mission. The prompt shows no content or digest.
- The approval is desktopRequired (bus.server.ts:171), so a device cannot answer it. Codex sessions map to "shell" (authorization.server.ts:201) and are refused for remote envelopes. Claude read sessions are refused too. So I found no device-only path to execution.
- Post-approval binding does hold: capabilityOperation (line 265) digests the named files via fileIdentities, so the grant fails if the file changes after the ask. This protects against a later swap, not against a blind approval.

Why HIGH rather than BLOCKER: execution needs a workstation user to allow_once a code-running request whose prompt names a device-written file. The review gate is the owner-accepted backstop, but the prompt does not show content, so the human cannot tell the file holds code. The (A) contract text and the accepted-limitation wording that assume inert files cannot be loaded as code must be corrected or the inertness rule tightened. Other routes I checked (for example .babelrc.json, .eslintrc.json or jest.config.json plugin or transform paths naming a .txt file) are also behind the same review gate, so they do not change severity.

Claim confirmed, not refuted. Verified in source: authorization.server.ts:126 INERT_DATA_FILE accepts .txt/.md/.log/.csv/.yaml; inertDataPath (line ~156) and remoteExecutionRefusal (line ~232) return null for filesystem.write to notes.txt, and the same for data.log and p.md. Probe in a mkdtemp folder (since deleted): classifier returns refusal=null, inert=true for all three; `node notes.txt` executed a device-style JS body and created PWNED.txt. So the (A) contract, that device-written files cannot be loaded as code, is false for interpreters. Chain: bus.server.ts:169 runsCode(terminal.exec) plus pendingRemoteReview (manager.server.ts ~2303) asks with desktopRequired and a reason that names only the changed path. The workstation allow_once grant binds fileIdentities digests (authorization.server.ts:245-265), so the bytes are pinned at ask time, but the human is never shown the contents. A device therefore gets device-authored code run on one workstation click with only a filename shown. The device cannot execute anything without that human allow, so I do not rate it a BLOCKER (no device-only path to execution). It is still a violation of the stated owner invariant and of the claim in the (A) contract and accepted-limitation text. I did not verify the Python claim, only the Node one. No repo files were modified and no repo tests were run, so test-results/ is unchanged.

finding.title: A retried or rerouted attempt's surviving descendants are dropped from the mid-run hold
finding.scenario: A Task's first attempt ends with a retryable failure (for example 'invalid json', classified MALFORMED_RESULT and retried on the same candidate). Attempt 1's root exits but a child process it started (node.exe) keeps running. The loop calls stopTree(id) at line 1423 but never calls watchSurvivors for the ended attempt. startSession then overwrites this.sessions with the new session (line 1345 and the reassignments at 1555, 1581, 1597). watchSurvivors runs only once, in the final finally at line 1644, using this.sessions.get(id), i.e. the last attempt. Attempt 1's live descendants therefore never enter tasks.lingering, so liveCodeExecutions (manager.server.ts:2311-2319) and the device hold (remoteMutationHeld, line ~2330) stop counting workstation-approved code that is still running. A paired-device Mission write or read-data change is no longer held while that process runs. The owner-approved (B) claim that each ended attempt keeps its own lineage, so a retry never hides an earlier attempt's survivors, is not what the code does.
finding.evidence: Probe (TaskManager only, fake claude adapter, processTable injected): attempt 1 pid 4242 with child 4343 (node.exe). After the attempt-1 finish and relaunch, tasks.lingering keys were []; the child was still alive in the table. After 11 s with attempt 2 running, lingering was still []. When the Task completed, lingering held only attempt-2's key ("<taskId>#1", pid 5242); attempt-1 child still alive. Test F01-R40 passes but calls watchSurvivors directly twice and never runs the completion loop, so it does not exercise this path. Test run: remote-authority.test.ts 60/60 pass. The mission-level hold was not separately probed; the conclusion rests on the shared liveCodeExecutions map.
finding.recommendation: Call this.watchSurvivors(id, <pid of the ended session>) for each attempt before the loop reassigns `session`, for example right after this.stopTree(id) at line 1423 with session.pid?.() ?? this.db.get(id).pid. Add a test that drives the real completion loop through a relaunch and asserts the earlier attempt's child is tracked.

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted. The mechanism is real, but the claimed HIGH severity is overstated.

Mechanism (code read, no probes or tests run; no repo files touched):
- manager.server.ts:1423 calls stopTree(id) at the top of the retry loop, and no watchSurvivors call exists in the loop. watchSurvivors appears only in the finally block (line 1644), where it uses this.sessions.get(id), which holds the last attempt's session.
- startSession overwrites this.sessions (line 1345 and the reassignments at 1555, 1581, 1597). The loop variable `session` is also reassigned, so attempt 1's root pid is not recorded anywhere.
- The retry is reachable. routing.server.ts:401-403 maps MALFORMED_RESULT to retry-same, so the same candidate is relaunched.
- Attempt 1's tree snapshot is replaced by attempt 2's watchTree tick (watchTree is re-armed via session.recorded at line 1234 after stopTree clears the timer). Attempt-1 descendants are therefore dropped from processTree and never enter a lineage.
- The consumer at missions/manager.server.ts:2311-2319 counts only this.tasks.sessions keys (live attempts, and only if shell-capable per providerSessionAuthority) and lingering keys. After the Task's finally runs, sessions.delete(id) executes, and the only lingering entry is for the last attempt's root closure. Attempt 1's orphan is therefore invisible to remoteMutationHeld (line 2322-2333) once the Task completes, and also while attempt 2 is tool-free or read-only (for example after a reroute to a non-shell provider).

Why severity is MEDIUM, not HIGH:
- The device still cannot place or load code (round-7 (A) contract holds), and writes remain bounded to exact planned Mission-envelope steps. The lost protection is the mid-run hold, which the owner's round-7 notes describe as defence in depth. The practical effect is that device-written inert data inside the envelope can reach a workstation-approved process that is still running and was observed by Bunny. This is a correctness gap against the owner's explicit (B) claim, not an escape from the envelope or code execution by a device.

Recommendation (agree with reporter): call watchSurvivors for each ended attempt before `session` is reassigned, for example right after stopTree at line 1423 using session.pid?.() ?? this.db.get(id).pid. Add a test that drives the completion loop through a relaunch.

The core claim holds, but I downgrade the severity to MEDIUM.

Verified by reading the code (no files written, no tests run):
- src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1423 is `this.stopTree(id)` in the completion loop. No watchSurvivors call sits on the retry, reroute, or escalate paths. The `continue` statements after startSession (about lines 1549, 1579, 1593) reassign `session` without tracking the ended attempt.
- watchSurvivors has a single call site, in the final finally (line 1644), and it uses `this.sessions.get(id)` at that point. That is the last attempt only, so attempt 1's root and its observed children never enter `lingering`.
- startSession (lines 1268-1345) overwrites this.sessions, and the only tree snapshots (watchTree, lines 1651-1700) are keyed to the current pid, so nothing else preserves attempt 1's lineage.

The finding also understates a second gap that the suggested fix does not close. liveCodeExecutions (src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:2311-2319) resolves each lingering or session key to `this.tasks.db.get(id).provider`, the CURRENT provider, and drops it when that provider's authority is tool_free or read_tools. startSession (line 1300-1305) rewrites task.provider on reroute. So if attempt 1 ran codex (shell) and a reroute moved the task to ollama (tool_free), a correctly tracked attempt-1 survivor would still be filtered out. The recommended watchSurvivors fix alone is therefore incomplete for reroute cases. It works for same-provider retries.

Why MEDIUM rather than HIGH: the bypass removes only the mid-run hold on device-attributable Mission mutations. A device can still write only bounded, exact planned inert data steps inside the envelope. It cannot place code, cannot launch anything, and cannot widen authority. The impact is a race on inert data read by an already-running workstation-approved descendant, and the review gate still covers any later launch. The owner's accepted-limitation list does not cover this case, because this process was observed. So it is a real correctness gap in a defence-in-depth control, not an owner-policy disposition.

Test coverage: remote-authority.test.ts:1290-1331 calls watchSurvivors directly and does not drive the completion loop, so the gap is not caught.

finding.title: Git reads are not covered by the mid-run hold; a device write can land while a workstation git read is running
finding.scenario: The review gate runs only at decision time for git.* reads (bus.server.ts:169 covers runsCode or git.*). runsCode (authorization.server.ts:237-238) is true only for terminal.exec, GIT_MUTATIONS and non-Calculator EXECUTE. So a workstation git.status is never placed in bus.liveCode (bus.server.ts:308), and remoteMutationHeld does not hold a paired-device write that is admitted while it runs. Git then reads that file under any owner-configured clean filter or textconv that applies to it, and the device content was never reviewed before the read.
finding.evidence: Probe (fake git adapter with a 2 s git.status execute, real MissionManager/TaskManager): the device write landed while git.status was still running (write completed, gitEnd === 0); liveCodeExecutions() was [] and bus.liveCode.size was 0. The change was recorded as pending only after the read had started. Exploitation depends on an owner-configured filter driver, which the accepted-limitations list already covers, so only the timing gap is new.
finding.recommendation: Treat git.* actions as code-running for liveCode and for remoteMutationHeld (add them to runsCode or to a separate liveCode predicate), so a device write waits until the in-flight git read ends.

votes.reasoning:
The gap is real in the code. bus.server.ts:308 adds a run to bus.liveCode only when runsCode() is true. runsCode (authorization.server.ts:237-238) covers terminal.exec, GIT_MUTATIONS and non-Calculator EXECUTE, so a READ-risk git.status/git.diff/git.log is never in liveCode. manager.server.ts:2311-2331 builds liveCodeExecutions() from bus.liveCode and shell-capable sessions only, and remoteMutationHeld() (manager.server.ts:2322) checks only that set. So a paired-device filesystem.write admitted while a git read is in flight is not held (bus.server.ts:165). The review gate at bus.server.ts:169 is decision-time only, so the in-flight read is not covered. The Git read path itself is not refuted: git status can run clean filters on files whose stat changed, and device-written files are not in the pending review at ask time.

Why severity is LOW and not MEDIUM or higher: the only code that runs is an owner-configured filter or textconv program (core.attributesFile, global or repo config). The device cannot write .gitattributes, .git/config or other execution-config files (authorization.server.ts:123-124, 229), and it does not choose the program. The device supplies only bytes to that owner program. That sits next to the accepted limitation "Git reads under remote authority run owner-configured filter drivers already present in repo/global config", so this adds only a timing gap for unreviewed content. It is not a device-chosen code execution path and does not reach the shell. Preconditions: an owner-configured filter that applies to the device-written file type, a device write timed inside a git read window, and a non-trivial repo (git.status must actually read the file). The fix in the recommendation (add git.* to liveCode or hold device writes during git reads) is sound and cheap.

No repo files were modified. I only ran Grep, Read and one read-only git diff --stat. No tests were run and no test-results files changed.

The core claim is confirmed by code reading. authorization.server.ts:237-238 runsCode() excludes git.* reads (terminal.exec, GIT_MUTATIONS and non-Calculator EXECUTE only). bus.server.ts:308 sets bus.liveCode only when runsCode() is true, so an in-flight git.status/git.diff is never in liveCode. manager.server.ts:2322-2334 remoteMutationHeld() consults only liveCodeExecutions() (bus.liveCode plus shell-capable sessions), and desktopExecutionConflict() covers only trusted-desktop executions. A device MUTATIONS write admitted during a workstation git read is therefore not held. The review gate at bus.server.ts:169 runs only at decision time, so the in-flight window is real. The git.* review comment at line 168 states the invariant that code never runs over unreviewed device changes, and this gap violates that invariant.

I probed the mechanism in a throwaway temp repo: a filter.probe.clean driver ran on a modified file during git status --porcelain (marker written), and did not run when the tree was unchanged. So git status does feed device-modified bytes to an owner-configured clean filter, which is the mechanism the finding relies on.

Severity is LOW, not MEDIUM. Impact needs an owner-configured clean/textconv filter (the accepted-limitation class), the device controls only input bytes to that owner program and cannot place or load code (filesystem.write remotely is inert-data only, per round-7 (A)), and the window is the duration of one read. The fix is still warranted: add git.* reads to the liveCode predicate or hold device mutations during them. Not refuted, because the in-flight gap is not covered by any listed disposition or accepted limitation.

Coverage: probe folder created under the OS temp dir and deleted afterwards. No repo file was edited. Only git commands were run in the temp repo. The repo test-results/ path shows no change. The remote-authority test was not run, since it was not needed for this probe.

finding.title: Inert-extension classifier is not a code-loading guarantee: .txt/.md/.log/.json etc. execute as JavaScript
finding.scenario: Round-7 fix (A) allows a paired device to write any file ending in .txt/.text/.md/.markdown/.csv/.tsv/.json/.jsonl/.ndjson/.yaml/.yml/.log under remote authority, on the stated premise that such files can never be loaded and run as code. Node does not honour that premise: a file named payload.txt with console.log is executed by `node payload.txt` (exit 0, printed), and `require('./lib.txt')` executes it as CommonJS (verified by a throwaway probe in a mkdtemp folder, since deleted). Config-style JSON files also name local modules that get loaded: .prettierrc.json plugins, .mocharc.json require, .eslintrc.json parser, babel.config.json plugins. So an inert .json config plus an inert .txt module forms an executable pair that the classifier allows. Device exploitability today: the device chooses no write content (planned steps carry their content; cross-app content is Agent-only and devices cannot approve Agent missions), so I found no device-triggered execution path from this. The invariant the owner relied on is nonetheless false, and the test pins the wrong contract.
finding.evidence: Probe: `node payload.txt` printed TXT-EXECUTED-AS-JS and `node -e require('./lib.txt')` ran the file. remoteExecutionRefusal('filesystem.write',{path:'notes.txt'},'WRITE',root) returns null (ALLOW); same for 'scripts/run.txt', 'tools/a.md', 'data.yml', 'x.log', 'babel.config.json', '.eslintrc.json'. Gate at authorization.server.ts:232 (`action === "filesystem.write" && !inertDataPath(path)`). Test remote-authority.test.ts:1307-1313 (F01-R39) asserts notes.txt, README.md, data/table.csv, out/result.json, conf/values.yaml, a/b.log are allowed and claims code is desktop-only.
finding.recommendation: Either narrow remote filesystem.write to an extension set that no runtime in this stack loads (drop .txt/.md/.log/.json from the write allowlist, or keep only content that is never required, e.g. .csv/.tsv/.log under a non-config folder), or document the residual explicitly as accepted and state that the review gate is the only control for loadable data files. Correct the F01-R39 assertions and the (A) premise text. Escalate to BLOCKER if any device-influenced content can reach a filesystem.write (for example a cross-app or model output path reachable from a device answer).

votes.reasoning:
Not refuted. The premise is false and the finding's core claim reproduces.

Probe (throwaway mkdtemp folder under the OS temp dir, deleted afterwards): lib.txt containing console.log("TXT-RAN") was loaded by a CJS main.cjs doing require("./lib.txt"). It printed TXT-RAN and exited 0. Node runs unknown extensions as CommonJS, so the inert-extension premise does not hold.

Code path confirmed: authorization.server.ts:232 gates filesystem.write only on inertDataPath(path). The regexes at authorization.server.ts:121-123 (INERT_DATA_FILE, AGENT_CONFIG_FILE) and EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE (line ~118) do not catch .mocharc.json, .eslintrc.json, babel.config.json or .txt modules. So a device can place a .mocharc.json with require ./hook.txt plus hook.txt, and both pass remoteExecutionRefusal. The comment at authorization.server.ts:230-231 ("nothing it writes can be loaded and run as code later") is therefore wrong. The test F01-R39 at remote-authority.test.ts:1307-1313 pins the wrong contract.

Mitigations that keep this at MEDIUM rather than HIGH or BLOCKER: manager.server.ts:2303-2310 (pendingRemoteReview) is a Host-wide review gate. Any code-running request waits for the workstation to acknowledge pending device changes. The prompt shows at most 12 paths, not file contents, so the workstation approves names it cannot inspect. Exploitation therefore needs a later workstation-approved code run that loads the planted file. A device cannot execute code directly, and the device picks no write content. The gap is a broken security invariant plus a weaker review than the owner assumed, not a direct device-triggered execution path. No change to repo files was made by me, and I did not run the repo test (coverage: no test-results changes from my work).

Not refuted. The core claim holds and is narrower than the finding's example.

Verified in code: authorization.server.ts:126 INERT_DATA_FILE includes txt|text|md|markdown|csv|tsv|json|jsonl|ndjson|yaml|yml|log. remoteExecutionRefusal (line 232) only checks inertDataPath plus the executionConfigPath denylist (line 230). EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE (line ~117) matches only *.config.[cm]?[jt]s, *rc.[cm]?[jt]s and similar JS/TS names, so babel.config.json, .eslintrc.json, .mocharc.json and tsconfig.json all pass as inert. A device-written .json config plus a device-written .txt module is therefore allowed. The (A) premise that such files "can never be loaded and run as code" is false.

Probe (mkdtemp under the OS temp dir, deleted afterwards, no repo files touched): in a package.json with "type":"module" (this repo's layout), `node payload.txt` and `import('./payload.txt')` both fail with ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION, so the finding's example does not reproduce here. However, `require('./lib.txt')` from a .cjs file executed the .txt body (printed TXT-REQUIRED, exit 0). So any CJS require-based loader that is pointed at a device-written .txt path runs it. The finding's exact "node payload.txt" evidence is only valid outside a type:module package.

Device path: remote Mission creation takes only an objective (manager/commands: explicit steps are workstation-only). The planner can make capability steps, so content is not strictly controlled by the device, and the device-created write path is plausible but I did not fully trace it. This is not a BLOCKER on current evidence: Bunny-launched code runs wait on the Host-wide pendingRemoteReview gate, which lists paths only. Direct (non-Mission) workstation runs and editors are outside that gate. In this repo's own scripts I found no obvious require-based consumer of .json/.txt config (scripts use node --test, tsc, eslint with flat config, vite), so present exploitability depends on an external tool, such as an editor loading tsconfig plugins, that I could not confirm. Hence MEDIUM. The test F01-R39 (remote-authority.test.ts:1307-1313) pins the wrong contract and needs correction.

finding.title: Mid-run hold ignores detached terminal.exec children, so device-attributable writes land while workstation-approved code still runs
finding.scenario: A workstation-approved terminal.exec whose command starts a detached process (for example Start-Process or `start /B` with redirected or closed stdio) returns normally. runCommand resolves on child 'close' with no tree reap (process.server.ts:83-86; taskkill /T runs only on timeout or abort). The bus then clears liveCode (bus.server.ts:349). Survivor tracking (watchSurvivors) is called only when a provider session ends (manager.server.ts:1644), never for terminal runs. liveCodeExecutions() therefore reports nothing, and remoteMutationHeld() lets paired-device filesystem.write/delete/download proceed while the detached workstation process is still live. finding.title: Remote write classifier allows config files that external tools execute, outside the Bunny review gate
finding.scenario: A paired device with a remote Mission envelope covering the project writes a root-level file such as .devcontainer.json, vercel.json, firebase.json, .huskyrc.json, .lintstagedrc.json, .gitlab-ci.yml or .circleci/config.yml. remoteExecutionRefusal returns null (inert .json/.yml name, no config dir or file match), so the write is allowed with no prompt and no desktop grant. Bunny's review gate only fires on code Bunny itself runs (terminal, provider sessions, git.commit/merge/worktree, Git reads), so if the owner then reopens the folder in a dev container (VS Code initializeCommand runs on the host), deploys (vercel buildCommand, firebase predeploy), commits outside Bunny (husky/lint-staged hooks) or pushes (CI), the device-authored commands run with no Bunny review. The denylist is accepted by design, but these names are not on it and the review gate cannot see their external triggers. Execution impact of each tool is from tool documentation, not run here; the classification result is probe-verified.
finding.evidence: Probe (node --experimental-strip-types, repo module imported by file URL, project root in a mkdtemp folder) of remoteExecutionRefusal('filesystem.write', {path, content}, 'WRITE', root) returned null (ALLOWED) for: .devcontainer.json, vercel.json, firebase.json, .huskyrc.json, .lintstagedrc.json, lint-staged.config.json, .gitlab-ci.yml, .circleci/config.yml, azure-pipelines.yml, docker-compose.json, package-lock.json, tsconfig.json, devcontainer.json. finding.title: Trusted-desktop grants minted for workstation-envelope asks are never consumed
finding.scenario: A desktopRequired review or mid-run-hold ask on a WORKSTATION envelope is answered allow_once; MissionManager.respond mints a grant (uses 0, 5-minute TTL). On re-execution the bus computes remote=false, so desktopGrantFor is never called and the grant is never consumed (consumption only occurs at line 299 when decision.desktopGrant is set, which requires the remote path). The grant stays unused and valid until expiry. A device cannot reach this path (desktopGrantFor and desktopCapabilityGrant are consulted only for remote envelopes, and an envelope's grantedBy is fixed), so no escalation was found. It does contradict the single-use statement on DesktopGrant.
finding.evidence: bus.server.ts:174 (const grant = remote ? this.desktopGrantFor?.(...) : null), :177 (grant only returned on remote path), :299 (consume only when decision.desktopGrant). manager.server.ts respond() mints for every desktopRequired allow_once regardless of envelope authority. Code reading only; not probed.
finding.recommendation: Either consume (or revoke) the grant on every path that resolves a desktopRequired ask, or document that workstation-envelope grants are advisory and never consulted. Consider revoking the grant when the step's approvedOnce is consumed.

finding.title: Inert-data classifier admits extensions Node executes as code; the (A) no-code-placement guarantee does not hold
finding.scenario: A paired device (remote envelope, or a single device answer on a workstation step) calls filesystem.write with path payload.txt and content `require('fs').writeFileSync('ran.flag','x')`. remoteExecutionRefusal returns null (allowed) because .txt matches INERT_DATA_FILE and no config rule applies. Node runs unknown extensions as CommonJS: `node payload.txt` and `require('./payload.txt')` both execute the JavaScript (verified on this machine with node 24; also verified for .md, .text, .markdown, .csv, .tsv, .log, .yaml, .yml, .jsonl). The same allowed set also covers config files that name a loader target without any denylist hit: .babelrc.json, .mocharc.json, .aider.conf.yml, GEMINI.md, and anything under .windsurf/ or .roo/ (none in EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE/_DIR or AGENT_CONFIG_FILE; probed: remoteExecutionRefusal('filesystem.write',{path},'WRITE',cwd) === null and executionConfigPath === false for all of them). Code the device placed therefore runs as soon as any workstation-approved command loads it (node <file>, mocha/babel config, etc.). The review gate lists the path in the workstation prompt, so this needs a workstation approval, but the round-7 contract 'a device can no longer place code that any later or already-running process could load' is false.
finding.evidence: Probe (mkdtemp, repo modules imported by file URL): inert=true execCfg=false remote=ALLOWED for payload.txt, notes.md, data.csv, helper.log, cfg/.mocharc.json, .babelrc.json, .aider.conf.yml, GEMINI.md, .windsurf/rules/r.md; helper.py and run.sh REFUSED. Gate code: line 232 `if (action === "filesystem.write" && !inertDataPath(path))`; line 123 EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE has no .babelrc*/.mocharc*/.aider* entries; line 127 AGENT_CONFIG_FILE lacks GEMINI.md and the .windsurf/.roo/.kiro directories are not in EXECUTION_CONFIG_DIR.
finding.recommendation: Remove from the remote-write allowlist every extension Node will execute (.txt .text .md .markdown .csv .tsv .log .yaml .yml .jsonl .ndjson), or keep only inert formats (.json is not executed by node or require), and add a regression that a remote-written file in the allowed set cannot be run by `node <file>` or required. finding.title: A device one-time answer on a workstation envelope still executes after the envelope expires
finding.scenario: Workstation-granted Mission (workstation envelope, not remote). A device answers allow_once for an in-scope bounded filesystem.write while the envelope is live (deviceRequestRefusal passes; it checks expiry only at answer time). The envelope then reaches expiresAt before the step runs (step is ready but not yet launched, or the Mission resumes later). decide() returns allow at line 373 because context.oneTime is checked before the workstation expiry check at line 381; the only expiry check before it (line 372) applies to remote envelopes. The file is written and the Mission keeps running under an expired authorization. Revocation is blocked by line 370, expiry is not. Device answers on remote envelopes are correctly blocked by line 372. The owner's accepted limitation covers only one-time answers given after expiry, not answers given before expiry and executed after it.
finding.evidence: Probe (mkdtemp, real HostDatabase/TaskManager/MissionManager, schedule paused until after the answer): workstation approval with alwaysAsk=['WRITE'] forced an ask 'write actions always ask.'; `mission.respond allow_once` by device:probe-phone -> ACCEPTED; then saveAuthorization with expiresAt = now-1000; realSchedule(missionId) -> mission state 'running', note.txt exists with content 'from device'. Same probe with a device answer after expiry is refused by deviceRequestRefusal (live.expiresAt <= Date.now()).
finding.recommendation: Apply the expiry check before the one-time allowance for every non-direct envelope (move the line-381 expiry test above line 373, or re-check expiresAt at execution in capabilityRequest/bus.request for oneTime paths), and add a regression that an approvedOnce step does not run after its envelope expires. If the owner decides workstation one-time answers should survive expiry, record that as an explicit decision distinct from device answers.
